comments.name: Aaron
comments.body: My problem with this opinion pieces—and of some of French’s assumptions—is that it seems like many conservatives equate a place where a multitude of different opinions run free as “liberal indoctrination”. I went to Harvard, graduated in 1995. I didn’t even know what politics any of my professors had. I didn’t even know what politics I had – or most of my fellow students had. Politics just didn’t matter much to us. We were interested in having debates and getting to the truth about things. Or at least coming to own conclusions about them. Topics included issues considered hot-button political footballs in the wider world: abortion, religion, American interventionism. But nobody was being indoctrinated. Our minds were being opened to myriad opinions from tons of bright young students and professors. I’ve had my issues with Harvard over the years—many of my fellow graduates can act arrogant and privileged. But anyone who has the opportunity and means to attend a school like Harvard should consider themselves lucky. I certainly do.

The technology is frightening, but the most important part of this story may be the institution wielding it. Russia did not need AI to erase the distinction between military and civilian targets. Give this army artillery, and it shells maternity hospitals and civilian infrastructure. Give it Shaheds, and apartment buildings become targets. Give it autonomous AI, and someone trains the system to recognize propane tanks at gas stations in a city full of civilians.

The instrument keeps changing; the ethics generating the target list do not. The AI did not lower anyone’s inhibitions. Those inhibitions had been eroded long before the chip arrived.

Nor did the AI decide that a propane tank at a civilian gas station was an acceptable target. Human beings determined what the system should recognize, where it should hunt and under what circumstances it could attack. What autonomy adds is scale, speed and potentially another layer of distance between those choices and the civilians who die from them.

That is why the debate over autonomous weapons cannot be only about the technology. We certainly need rules governing machines that can select and engage targets without human intervention. But regulating the machine without reckoning with the military institution wielding it mistakes the instrument for the actor.

The frightening thing here isn’t that the machine developed Russian rules of engagement. It was taught them.

These interceptors could become one layer of a broader defense.

Imagine an imminent attack on a U.S. base, city, reservoir or power grid. Launchers could release thousands of drones, coordinated like a civilian light show but assigned defensive roles. Some detect threats through radar, radio and optical sensors. Others relay data, jam guidance or generate false radar and heat signatures based on chaff, flares and towed decoys. A final group intercepts incoming drones. Together, they form a shifting aerial web instead of firing one costly missile at each cheap target.

Pieces already exist. Interceptor drones are used against Shaheds in Ukraine and produced for Middle Eastern defenses. Autonomous formation flight has been demonstrated. Electronic warfare disrupts drone communications and navigation; ground-based lasers and high-powered microwaves are being tested. The next step is integrating them into a network. Powerful lasers should remain mainly on land or ships, where energy and cooling are available, while drones supply targeting data. The result could resemble the webbed dome of protection once confined to science fiction.

Unarmed variants could deliver blood, medicine, water-purification supplies, food and communications equipment after disasters. Drones already transport vaccines, blood products and diagnostic samples to remote regions, while companies test food and package delivery. A national drone reserve could strengthen military defense and disaster response.

The only reason classical music has deified its interpreters (performers) and teachers of interpretations is that until recently, composers did not have the technology, the tools as the other arts had, to create their one product from their unique inspiration. They didn’t have their slab of granite or palette of colors. They could only leave instructions – notes, speed, rhythm, volume, cues to expressiveness, instrumentation – for others to follow. In other words, we've all been deluded to think that a piece of music exists only in someone's interpretation, not in itself.

If Guillaume Dufay and Josquin des Prez or the creators of Gregorian Chant had had tape recorders, we would now have a conception of music that was parallel universe-different from the historical one. We would all be listening to the one recording of Bach’s Mass in B minor and Chopin’s Barcarolle, produced by those geniuses themselves; buying or hearing in museums facsimiles of the one rare masterpiece. Pianists and flutists and clarinetists and conductors would be rid of their pretensions and off their cushioned butts, happy to be composing and teaching. I've seen all of Kathryn Bigelow's films at least once, including her early experimental film "The Set-Up" at a MoMA screening.  There is an unmistakable and coherent through-line at the heart of all of her movies.  She always asks: What's really going on inside a human facing oblivion?  Who is he in that moment?  Does the brain shut off - is the self erased? - or does it go into overdrive?  And what's the appeal of that danger?  How does it keep drawing him back in?

Certainly, she is responsible for a diverse body of work, and some of her films don't fully succeed, but these questions are always there whether her subject is a cop, a terrorist, a vampire, a soldier, or an extreme surfer.  She's the most skilled director of high-adrenaline action sequences because she gives the audience a real and overwhelming sense of that rush.  If you watched in slow-motion, for example, the skydiving sequences in Point Break or the finales of Strange Days and Zero Dark Thirty, you'd quickly see just how meticulous she is and why she leaves most action movies in the dust.

And because it's the most breathless of all her movies, Point Break might be the perfect encapsulation of the Bigelow thesis.  If you had time to think, you might realize how outrageous the whole situations is, but instead, you lose yourself in the ecstasy of lust and peril. It's no wonder that we're all as addicted to Point Break as Bodhi is to the waves!

Drilling rigs do not “extract oil and gas.” They drill holes, a process that typically takes about three weeks. Drilling rigs typically spend about three weeks at drilling sites and are removed before the extraction process begins.

The new technology that permits oil companies to extract oil and gas from shale formations is directional drilling, not fracking. Directional drilling  permits drillers to drill horizontally as well as vertically though oil bearing shale formations like miners following a seam of coal.  Hydraulic  fracking was first introduced in 1949. Fracking did not make drilling oils wells in shale profitable until it was used in combination with directional drilling.

People who drill wells and extract the oil and gas are not frackers. Fracking crews and pump trucks owned by oil field service supply companies typically spend one or two days at a well head.

It is the absence, not the presence, that should be remembered most. That is what makes the two empty spaces at the site so meaningful. Experience the absence, yes. Buy a t shirt or a hat, no. Smile for a photograph at the site, no. For me, one of the most poignant memories was of  the cars left in commuter parking lots near train stations in Summit, New Jersey and other locations in the area, the reminders of local residents who commuted to or through the World Trade Center that day and never returned.

My cousins are harvesting durum in North Dakota as I write, and I'll be there myself in a week to "help" (try not to get in the way).  My comment is a nit, but one which 99% of journalists get wrong: grain is not stored in silos, it is stored in grain bins and grain elevators.  If it's a major transshipment point it may be referred to as a grain terminal.  A silo has an entirely different function, that is to store green fodder crops in anaerobic conditions where it will ferment and become highly nutritious livestock feed, or silage.  In my life I have operated combines harvesting small grains, and forage harvesters chopping corn for silage, they each have their storage facilities and they are definitely not interchangeable. I'm not mentioning missile silos (plentiful in North Dakota) as their contents are generally considered inedible.

From the article: “In addition to harming respiratory health, those fires also produce disproportionately large greenhouse emissions because peatland stores far more carbon than forests.”

This is what worries me in particular about these fires is that they are turning important carbon sinks into net emitters of carbon dioxide (CO2, a greenhouse gas).

The 2023 Canadian wildfires released more CO2 than the rest of Canadian sources combined (37 million acres burned). Climate models did not project fires like that until much later this century.

And recently this paper reported that the permafrost region has shifted from an important carbon sink into a net emitter of greenhouse gases, CO2 and methane.

Some natural systems like forests and frozen soils which minimized some of the impacts of our atmospheric experiment with our only planet are changing from being our friends to our enemies.

It's an interesting genre -- these authors need to react to the fact that Iceland is so safe and build a plausible story of crime, killing and deception. Although murder is rare, Iceland has never gotten over some of its most confusing disappearances. There's a lot to go on, even if there's not a lot of actual violent crime.

comments.name: Jim Brokaw
comments.body:
The United States has funded and fought a "War on Drugs" for over 50 years. The focus has always been on cutting supply, not on dealing with demand.

The falling price and widespread availability of hard drugs makes it clear that the "War on Drugs" has been as miserable a failure as the most recent Trump War in Iran. Hundreds of Billions of dollars spent on fighting the "War on Drugs", and the result is drugs more available, more potent, and less expensive than when it was started. Maybe it's time to try something different, and refocus on cutting some of the demand, instead of 95% of the funding going to interdicting the supply. No effort to interdict supply will succeed as long as the demand stays strong... the results of the last 50 years proves that.

comments.name: E R
comments.body: In  February my95 year old mom had a bowel surgery. It cleared her obstruction but shut down her kidneys and the 6 inch incision was not healing.They had to open it up to heal from the inside. After some dialysis, with no kidney improvement we took her home in hospice to say goodbye to her friends and die. But she wasn’t cooperating. She lay in the bed, existing with 24 hour help. I dug out of storage a rebounder I had given my parents 20 years ago. Every time I visited I had her sit at the edge of her bed with her feet on the trampoline mat while I bounced for a few minutes. We noticed that after I visited and made her do this that her urine volume quadrupled that night. The aides always measured this when they emptied the bag from her catheter. With this evidence of improvement the aides began doing the rebounding sessions with her when i was not there. These rebounding sessions kept her from holding fluid in her legs, and kept her hip knee and ankle joints mobile. I believe that they also helped her kidneys regain their full function. Once we found the miracle of eating a single oyster each day, her wound began healing at warp speed. The wound nurses who came twice a week to measure and clean it could not believe their eyes. Now my mom is out of the bed, walking with a walker, and getting back to her busy social life. She still rebounds with me and her number one aide. Sometimes she is standing on it herself ah gently bouncing as she holds the handle.

comments.name: Gandalf the Blue
comments.body:
Good recap, Noel.

I continue to like this adult (and R-rated) take on Green Lantern, just like I enjoyed HBO's version of "The Watchmen."

Hal Jordan is cocky or something to the point of being obnoxious, but Kyle Chandler plays him with such roguish charm that you have to love him.

They need to do more with John Stewart's character. Has to be getting time for a flashback to show how he teamed up with Hal in the first place. But great action scene with him this week, as you mentioned.

And good pickup on Sheriff Kane's possible real identity. I don't know about this version of the DC World, but in the one I read comics about as a kid, Green Lantern was part of the Justice League, along with Superman, Batman, Flash, Green Arrow, uhhhh, maybe Hawkman. Did Batwoman ever join the League? I can't recall, and I stopped reading comics after about 1970. That would be a cool surprise if the Sheriff turns into a @$$-kicking crimefighter a la her more famous male wearer of the cowl and cape.

And speaking of costumes, loved seeing Hal in the Green Arrow costume!

Oh, one last thing: "Hal makes a joke about how Nebraskans worship Tom Osborne." Like how Hoosiers used to worship Bobby Knight. And Ohioans used to worship Woody Hayes. And Floridians used to worship...Bobby Bowden? I forget. The point is that America has come to worship sports: the players and coaches of their favorite teams are like gods to them. A bit of satire about that in this episode, methinks.
